video_title: Erlina Yeo Terwelp: From Banking to PE to Family Office to Columbia Endowment
gist: Erlina Yeo Terwelp, Columbia endowment MD overseeing privates, says Columbia is growing private markets on offense (little legacy venture, ample unfundeds, publics have outrun privates) while guarding against 2026 venture/AI froth via vintage diversification and concentration monitoring. In buyouts she flags higher rates as the main tail risk, favoring operational value creation and HALO (high asset, low obsolescence) strategies, and describes Columbia's early risk-factor/equity-beta approach that predated TPA. Note: interviewer is a guest host (thanked as 'Hank'), not Ted Seides.

themes.theme: Private markets positioning: offense amid liquidity worries

insights.claim: Columbia's endowment still believes in private markets and is actively growing its private portfolio despite the industry-wide liquidity squeeze from companies staying private longer and fewer exits/distributions.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: A large endowment is a net buyer of private exposure while many peers are liquidity-constrained, supporting GP fundraising and secondary-pricing resilience.
insights.quote: the attractiveness of private markets is very much still there. So we believe in it. We're growing it.

insights.claim: Columbia is liquidity-advantaged versus peers because it entered the 2020s with very little venture exposure, does not have a huge illiquid portfolio, and holds a comfortable level of unfunded commitments.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Endowments that were underweight venture into the 2021 peak now have dry powder to deploy into a dislocated private market.
insights.quote: we actually have a very comfortable amount of unfundeds today

insights.claim: Because public markets have significantly outrun private markets, Columbia sees room to keep growing its private allocation and says it is positioned for offense rather than defense.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: The denominator effect has reversed: strong public equity returns create allocation headroom for privates.
insights.quote: especially as private public markets have really outrun private markets

insights.claim: Columbia has been doing a lot of co-investment this year, making it a meaningful use of the private team's time.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Co-invest is a key tool for LPs to deploy capital at lower fees and tilt exposure in the current private-markets environment.
insights.quote: we've been doing a lot of co-invest this year.

themes.theme: Venture froth, AI vintage risk and concentration

insights.claim: Terwelp describes 'some insanity' in venture in 2026, with many funds raising and companies raising at valuations that are multiples of where they priced about six months earlier.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Rapid step-ups in venture valuations signal late-cycle froth; underwriting assumptions for 2026 vintage should be conservative.
insights.quote: with so many companies raising at uh valuations that are uh you know multiples of what they just graced about 6 months ago

insights.claim: Vintage-year diversification is the most crucial defense right now: Columbia does not want to concentrate in a 2026 AI-euphoric vintage and wants exposure to 2027 and 2028 vintages too, since the next Nvidia may not be built until 2028.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Pace commitments steadily rather than front-loading into the hottest AI vintage; the biggest AI winners may come later.
insights.quote: we don't want to put all your eggs in a 2026 bucket. uh where people feel really good about AI

insights.claim: She expects fortunes to be made in the 2026 AI vintage, but believes later vintages may produce the defining companies.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Bullish on AI value creation but agnostic on timing; argues for continued multi-year deployment.
insights.quote: maybe the next Nvidia is not going to be built till 2028

insights.claim: A key left-tail risk in Columbia's venture book is concentration in the same widely held companies, raising groupthink risk even though some are 'spectacular' generational companies.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Crowded cap tables of consensus winners create correlated downside across LP portfolios; check look-through overlap across managers.
insights.quote: I also worry a little bit about group think

insights.claim: To manage venture concentration, Columbia aggregates look-through company exposure across managers and makes explicit judgment calls about whether to add to or trim over-represented names.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Look-through exposure analysis is a practical LP tool to avoid unintentional single-name bets via multiple funds.

insights.claim: Columbia's venture portfolio has shifted from being heavily biotech in the early 2020s to a much smaller biotech share today, with tech versus biotech an explicit tilt it monitors.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Signals reduced LP appetite for biotech VC relative to tech; biotech VC managers may face tougher fundraising.
insights.quote: a lot of the VC that we came in with in the 2020s was biotech um and that's been a small much smaller part of our VC portfolio today

themes.theme: Buyout underwriting in a higher-rate world

insights.claim: Higher interest rates are the biggest left-tail risk for buyouts because they change deal math, making revenue growth and margin expansion far more important to returns.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Leverage-driven PE returns are impaired; favor managers with demonstrated operational value creation.
insights.quote: The biggest one particularly for buyout is higher interest rates. It makes the math different.

insights.claim: Columbia now re-underwrites buyout managers on the value creation bridge (leverage, operating margins/growth, multiple expansion) and favors firms that have proven value creation in the operating piece, with a repeatable, durable playbook.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Ask GPs to decompose returns; discount returns driven by leverage and multiple expansion.
insights.quote: We really like firms that have proven a lot of value in the mult in the operating piece of it.

insights.claim: Five years ago Columbia deliberately set out to build a durable buyout portfolio, adding a healthy and growing allocation to HALO (high asset, low obsolescence) strategies rather than relying only on tech buyouts.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: HALO (hard-asset, low-obsolescence) buyouts are positioned as a hedge against concentrated tech/AI venture bets and AI disruption.
insights.quote: the high asset low obsolescence type uh strategies um uh the halo strateg IES

insights.claim: The HALO buyout allocation is explicitly intended to act as a buffer against the concentrated bets in the venture portfolio.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Pairing hard-asset buyouts with AI-heavy venture is a deliberate intra-private diversification approach.
insights.quote: So that does act as a buffer to some of the bets that we feel are very concentrated

insights.claim: Sector-specialist buyout firms (e.g., healthcare or consumer) can have operational edge because they repeat the same playbook, know the executives and reputations in their arena, and have 'seen the same movie before.'
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Specialization is a source of operating alpha in a world where financial engineering is less effective.
insights.quote: you get really good at executing the same playbook. you've seen a lot of the same movie before.

insights.claim: Buy-and-build is a widely claimed but very hard strategy because integration is difficult; she presses managers with many follow-up questions, but those who execute well can generate exceptional results.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of roll-up pitches; verify integration capability before underwriting multiple-arbitrage stories.
insights.quote: people say they did dream buy and build. Um, I always have a lot of follow-up questions because it's such a it's such a difficult strategy to execute.

insights.claim: She sees the era of low interest rates as over, calling it 'the olden days', and frames the current environment as a new world order shaped by AI disruption and fast change.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Strategies dependent on cheap money need re-underwriting; adaptation speed becomes an allocator edge.
insights.quote: The olden days of uh of uh you know uh low interest rates and uh certain certain things that we've been used to in the last 10 20 years are are just not there anymore.

insights.claim: Years before 'total portfolio approach' became common vernacular, Columbia managed its portfolio through risk factor allocation, managing to an equity beta target or range as dynamic risk management, much like a hedge fund.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: TPA's core idea (managing to equity beta rather than asset buckets) has a long track record at Columbia; peers adopting TPA are catching up.
insights.quote: It was less common back then to manage to an equity beta or a range as more of a form of dynamic risk management which I think that's what TPA is bringing into the system.

insights.claim: Under the generalist risk-factor model, every opportunity was evaluated in its cleanest form (equity beta, liquidity and its cost, leverage) with very little bucket filling and a bottom-up, first-principles approach.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Comparing all investments on beta, liquidity, and leverage avoids filling allocation buckets with mediocre managers.
insights.quote: it was very little bucket filling it was very much a bottoms up let's talk about let's go back to the first principles of what an investment was

insights.claim: She believes TPA is very difficult to apply to some private markets and private asset classes, even though it works well on the public side.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: TPA adopters should be cautious about the false precision of beta estimates for illiquid assets.
insights.quote: I think TPA is very difficult to do with uh some private markets and some private asset classes

insights.claim: Columbia frames portfolio construction as a set of explicit tilts (geography, early versus late stage, specialist versus generalist, tech versus biotech) rolled up from each asset class to the total portfolio; it is currently very US-tilted and debates whether that is acceptable given American exceptionalism.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: US concentration across asset classes is a conscious, debated bet at a major endowment; watch for any ex-US rebalancing.
insights.quote: our portfolio in general is very use tilted. Are we okay with that?

insights.claim: Moving from generalist to asset-class specialist taught her that portfolio construction, planning tilts and researching areas to inject into a portfolio, was the piece she had most underappreciated.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Specialist structures add deliberate portfolio planning that pure manager-picking generalist models can miss.

insights.claim: Under CIO Kim Lew, Columbia shifted from a generalist structure to specialists (two on privates, two on publics) while retaining generalist heritage: every fund is still discussed by the whole team.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Hybrid specialist/generalist structure is a template for small endowment teams; she calls the dichotomy false.
insights.quote: we still keep a lot of generalist heritage so uh you know we discuss every fund together

insights.claim: She argues there is little fundamental difference between evaluating a business and a fund manager: both require assessing the beta they are in, edge, positioning, moats, and the leadership team's ability to hire, inspire and execute.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Direct-investing skills transfer to LP work; treat GPs as businesses.
insights.quote: I don't think there is a huge huge difference in the fundamentals of what you're looking at between a business and and a manager.

insights.claim: Columbia's diligence process runs from a team-wide one-pager to a five-pager on the roughly five make-or-break questions unique to each investment, then a final investment proposal, mirroring the process at Catterton.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Focusing diligence on a handful of decisive questions is more productive than exhaustive checklists.
insights.quote: I believe that there's probably five things unique to every every investment that will make or break the deal.

insights.claim: Off-list references only work with warm connectivity; roughly 70% of the time Columbia's references come through people it already knows, and it has declined funds due to a very negative, corroborated off-list reference.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: LP network depth is a real diligence edge; cold reference calls rarely surface the truth.
insights.quote: I mean we have absolutely said no to funds um because of an offus reference that we got that was

insights.claim: The top reason Columbia exits a manager is fund size growing beyond what suits the strategy, which raises the question of whether the GP is now chasing AUM rather than returns, though even doubling or tripling fund size is not an automatic no.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Fund-size creep is the main signal of style drift; analyze capacity rather than reflexively exiting.
insights.quote: are you now searching for AUM versus returns um question

insights.claim: The second exit trigger is a manager late in its life cycle, marked by high turnover and carry allocated in ways that don't reflect where the talent is, independent of track record.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Carry distribution and turnover are leading indicators of future GP performance that past returns won't show.
insights.quote: you have a lot of turnover you have carry that's allocated in ways that we don't think reflects uh you know the talent that's in your organization

insights.claim: The third, rarest exit trigger is a red flag: a manager sending inaccurate information, since honesty and transparency are core to the relationship.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Integrity breaches are terminal regardless of performance.

insights.claim: Portfolio-level overweights (e.g., too many tech buyout managers) usually lead Columbia to trim commitments at the margin or not add new managers, with larger cuts happening only during broader portfolio reviews.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: Re-ups from large LPs in crowded sub-strategies may be smaller even for well-regarded GPs.
insights.quote: if we have too many, I don't know, tech buyout managers, maybe we won't add a bunch more.

insights.claim: Her biggest pet peeve is intellectual dishonesty, including people mistaking identifying risks for a lack of conviction; she tells her team she'd be upset if they don't find warts in a deal.
insights.speaker: Erlina Yeo Terwelp (Columbia Investment Management)
insights.so_what: A strong investment culture rewards surfacing risks rather than selling the deal.
insights.quote: people mistake risk for lack of conviction, identifying risks for lack of conviction
